blocks.text: **Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS)** is an acute immune attack on peripheral nerves, often after an infection. It causes rapidly progressive, usually symmetrical weakness starting in the legs and ascending, with reduced or absent reflexes. Breathing and swallowing muscles can become involved. Most patients recover over months, but some have lasting weakness and fatigue [Ref – to verify].

**Peripheral neuropathy** is damage to peripheral nerves from causes such as diabetes (most common), alcohol, vitamin B12 deficiency, chemotherapy, kidney disease or hereditary disease. It typically starts in the feet (length-dependent, "stocking" then "glove" distribution), with numbness, burning pain, loss of balance and later weakness.

rows: Distal sensory loss in feet, later hands

blocks.text: GBS: recent infection, speed of progression, breathing difficulty, swallowing, pain. Neuropathy: diabetes control, foot wounds, falls, burning pain, alcohol, medication history.

sections.title: D to E. Examination and measures

rows: Detect respiratory decline; falling vital capacity needs urgent medical review [Ref – to verify threshold]
Monofilament test (10 g) on the soles
Loss of protective sensation [Ref – to verify]
Vibration sense (128 Hz tuning fork) at the big toe
Proprioceptive balance: much worse with eyes closed suggests sensory ataxia

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Falling vital capacity, weak cough, swallowing difficulty in GBS
Large swings in heart rate and BP in GBS
Foot wound, redness, swelling in diabetic neuropathy
Hot, swollen, red foot without much pain in diabetes

items: Acute: respiratory monitoring, chest care, positioning, passive range, splints to prevent contracture, pain management through the team.

Recovery: gradual strengthening, avoiding excessive fatigue (short sessions, rest breaks), progressive mobility, balance and endurance training. Overwork weakness may occur, so progress carefully [Ref – to verify].
Balance training (static to dynamic, eyes open to closed, firm to soft surface).
Strength training for ankles and hips.
Aerobic exercise (improves glucose control in diabetes).
Daily foot checks, proper footwear, avoid barefoot walking.
Use vision and handrails at night; good lighting.

blocks.text: GBS: vital capacity, MRC sum score, GBS disability scale, walking. Neuropathy: balance measures, falls, foot condition.

items: **What is the most dangerous early complication of GBS?** Respiratory failure.
**Why is the Romberg test useful in neuropathy?** Large worsening with eyes closed shows reliance on vision due to lost proprioception.
**Why avoid over-fatiguing GBS patients?** Excessive exercise may cause prolonged fatigue and weakness.
**What does a positive monofilament test indicate?** Loss of protective sensation and higher ulcer risk.
**A diabetic patient has a hot swollen foot after a minor twist. What must be excluded?** Charcot foot and infection.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Plan balance, strength and foot protection for neuropathy.
